claim: TCRβ CDR3 sequences obtained from splenic CD4+ T cells from 12 healthy C57BL/6 mice had an average of about 30,000 different CDR3 sequences per mouse.
source: We obtained on average about 30,000 different CDR3 sequences from each mouse, which were found at varying abundances and had an average length of 13.4 ± 1.4 (mean ±SD) AA.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of sequences obtained from experimental data.

claim: The average length of CDR3 sequences from splenic CD4+ T cells from C57BL/6 mice was 13.4 ± 1.4 amino acids.
source: We obtained on average about 30,000 different CDR3 sequences from each mouse, which were found at varying abundances and had an average length of 13.4 ± 1.4 (mean ±SD) AA.
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the measured average length of CDR3 sequences.

claim: Networks formed by the thousand most frequent CDR3 sequences from a single mouse correspond to 34% of the total sequences obtained for that mouse.
source: Figure 1A shows a network obtained using the thousand most frequent CDR3 sequences from a single mouse, which in terms of abundance correspond to 34% of the total sequences obtained for that mouse.
evidence: The manuscript states this percentage and Figure 1A shows the corresponding network.

claim: CDR3 sequences (nodes) were connected by edges if they were separated by one amino acid difference (Levenshtein distance of 1).
source: CDR3 sequences (nodes) were connected (by edges) if they were separated by one amino acid difference (replacement/addition/ deletion of one AA) – a Levenshtein distance of 1(Levenshtein, 1966).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the edge connection criterion and cites the Levenshtein distance method.

claim: A cluster was defined as a set of two or more nodes that are connected to each other by any number of edges and intermediate nodes.
source: A cluster was defined as a set of two or more nodes that are connected to each other by any number of edges and intermediate nodes (Figure 1A, inset).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines what constitutes a cluster and references Figure 1A inset.

claim: B-cell immunoglobulin heavy-chain networks have been attributed to clonally derived sequences generated by somatic hyper-mutations.
source: A similar analysis had previously revealed the existence of networks of B-cell immunoglobulin heavy-chains, which were attributed to clonally derived sequences generated by somatic hyper-mutations (SHM) (Ben-Hamo and Efroni, 2011; Bashford-Rogers et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites previous studies that attributed BCR networks to somatic hypermutation.

claim: T cells do not undergo somatic hypermutation.
source: As T cells do not undergo SHM, other factors lead to the formation of TCR similarity networks.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established knowledge about T cell biology.

claim: Of the thousand most frequent CDR3 sequences in each mouse, 647 ± 104 (mean ±SD) were clustered, with 1282 ± 383 edges.
source: We repeated this analysis for all 12 mice, and found that of the thousand most frequent CDR3 sequences in each mouse (with an accumulated frequency of 34.5 ± 8% of total sequences), 647 ± 104 (mean ±SD) were clustered, with 1282 ± 383 edges.
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistics from analysis of 12 mice.

claim: Networks composed of a thousand randomly selected CDR3 sequences from a single mouse were much sparser than networks of the most frequent sequences, with only 225 ± 64 sequences clustered and 152 ± 52 edges.
source: In contrast, networks composed of a thousand randomly selected CDR3 sequences from a single mouse (with an accumulated frequency of 5 ± 0.7% of total sequences) were much sparser (Figure 1B), with only 225 ± 64 sequences clustered, and with 152 ± 52 edges (average values for 10 independent randomized sets of sequences).
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistics from randomized control analysis and references Figure 1B.

claim: There is no correlation (R2 = 0.11 ± 0.07) between the abundance of a TCR CDR3 sequence and its degree of connectivity in the network.
source: However, we found no correlation (R2 = 0.11 ± 0.07) between the abundance of a TCR CDR3 sequence and its degree of connectivity in the network (number of edges connecting it to other sequences).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation coefficient from statistical analysis.

claim: Each cluster typically contained sequences of a single (or in some cases two) specific J segment.
source: We further found that each cluster typically contained sequences of a single (or in some cases two) specific J segment (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: V usage in clusters was not cluster-specific; any cluster contained sequences with many different V segments.
source: V usage, in contrast, was not cluster-specific; any cluster contained sequences with many different V segments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pattern of clusters with homogenous J-gene and heterogeneous V-gene usage reflects the higher number of V segments compared with J segments.
source: This reflects the higher number of V segments compared with J segments, as well as their lower overlap with CDR3 and the relative similarity of their 3' ends.
evidence: The manuscript provides this explanation based on known properties of V and J segments.

claim: Networks of similar connectivity were obtained for the top 1000 CDR3β sequences from CD8 T cells.
source: Networks of similar connectivity were obtained also for the top 1000 CDR3β sequences from CD8 T cells, and for CD4 T cells of a different mouse strain (C3H.HeSnJ), that bears a different MHC haplotype (H2k; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supporting figures.

claim: Networks of similar connectivity were obtained for CD4 T cells of a different mouse strain (C3H.HeSnJ) that bears a different MHC haplotype (H2k).
source: Networks of similar connectivity were obtained also for the top 1000 CDR3β sequences from CD8 T cells, and for CD4 T cells of a different mouse strain (C3H.HeSnJ), that bears a different MHC haplotype (H2k; Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supporting figures.

claim: The most abundant CDR3 sequences formed connected clusters in human TCRβ repertoires.
source: We found a parallel network organization also in human TCRβ repertoires: we analyzed previously published data containing the TCRβ repertoires of 39 human subjects of different ages (Britanova et al., 2014), and found that the most abundant CDR3 sequences formed connected clusters in human TCR repertoires (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), though with a lower connectivity than that found in the similarity networks of inbred mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from analysis of published human data and references Figure 1C.

claim: Human TCR networks have lower connectivity than those found in inbred mice.
source: We found a parallel network organization also in human TCRβ repertoires: we analyzed previously published data containing the TCRβ repertoires of 39 human subjects of different ages (Britanova et al., 2014), and found that the most abundant CDR3 sequences formed connected clusters in human TCR repertoires (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), though with a lower connectivity than that found in the similarity networks of inbred mice.
evidence: The manuscript compares human and mouse network connectivity.

claim: From the thousand most frequent CDR3 sequences in each of the 11 young human subjects (ages 6–25 years), 207 ± 79 nodes were clustered, with 367 ± 201 edges.
source: From the thousand most frequent CDR3 sequences (accumulated frequency of 17.1 ± 6.6% of total sequences) in each of the 11 young human subjects in that study (ages 6–25 years), 207 ± 79 nodes were clustered, with 367 ± 201 edges.
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistics from analysis of human data.

claim: Networks composed of randomly selected sequences from individual human subjects generated only 8 ± 4 clustered nodes with 4 ± 2 edges.
source: Networks composed of randomly selected sequences from the individual subjects generated only 8 ± 4 clustered nodes with 4 ± 2 edges.
evidence: The manuscript reports these statistics from randomized control analysis of human data.

claim: TCR similarity networks are likely to be driven by conserved evolutionary forces, as opposed to BCR networks that are generated by SHM that operates within individuals.
source: We thus conclude that these newly discovered TCR similarity networks are likely to be driven by conserved evolutionary forces, as opposed to BCR networks that are generated by SHM that operates within individuals.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion based on comparison with BCR networks and the cross-species conservation of TCR networks.

claim: There is a strong association between the sharing level of a CDR3 sequence and its connectivity in the network: highly shared sequences are positioned at the center of network clusters.
source: Interestingly, we found a strong association between the sharing level of a CDR3 sequence and its connectivity in the network: highly shared sequences are positioned at the center of network clusters (Figure 1A).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 1A.

claim: There is a statistically significant correlation (R = 0.69 ± 0.03, p-value<2.2e-16) between the degree of node connectivity and its sharing level.
source: This is indicated by a statistically significant correlation between the degree of node connectivity (number of edges connecting it to other nodes in the network) and its sharing level (Figure 1D), (R = 0.69 ± 0.03, p-value<2.2e-16; see also Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports the correlation coefficient and p-value from statistical analysis and references Figure 1D.

claim: Betweenness centrality confirmed the correlation between CDR3 sharing and centrality for the 1000 most abundant CDR3 sequences, but not for a random set of expressed sequences.
source: An independent method for estimation of node centrality, betweenness centrality, confirmed the correlation between CDR3 sharing and centrality for the 1000 most abundant CDR3 sequences, but not for a random set of expressed sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 5, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding using an alternative centrality measure and references Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Public CDR3 sequences in humans manifested a higher degree of connectivity than did more private sequences.
source: As in mice, public CDR3 sequences in humans manifested a higher degree of connectivity than did more private sequences (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6), and sequence abundance was not correlated with its level of connectivity (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding for human data and references supporting figures.

claim: In humans, sequence abundance was not correlated with its level of connectivity.
source: As in mice, public CDR3 sequences in humans manifested a higher degree of connectivity than did more private sequences (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 6), and sequence abundance was not correlated with its level of connectivity (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding for human data.

claim: Public sequences are highly connected to other similar sequences and are more central in network clusters.
source: Thus, private and public CDR3 sequences are distributed differently across the mouse and human networks: public sequences are highly connected to other similar sequences and are more central in network clusters; in contrast, more private sequences are found at the edges of clusters, or as un-connected nodes, with rare similarity to other sequences in the network.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the differential distribution of public vs. private sequences in networks.

claim: Private sequences are found at the edges of clusters, or as un-connected nodes, with rare similarity to other sequences in the network.
source: Thus, private and public CDR3 sequences are distributed differently across the mouse and human networks: public sequences are highly connected to other similar sequences and are more central in network clusters; in contrast, more private sequences are found at the edges of clusters, or as un-connected nodes, with rare similarity to other sequences in the network.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the differential distribution of public vs. private sequences in networks.

claim: Out of 5,247,785 unique AA sequences in the human dataset (11 young individuals) and 371,977 in the mouse dataset (28 animals), 27,337 were shared by at least one mouse and one human individual.
source: Out of 5,247,785 unique AA sequences in the human dataset (11 young individuals) and 371,977 in the mouse dataset (28 animals), 27,337 were shared by at least one mouse and one human individual.
evidence: The manuscript reports these counts from cross-species comparison of sequence data.

claim: CDR3 sequences with a higher level of sharing in mice were found to have an increased probability of being found in human repertoires.
source: In general, CDR3 sequences with a higher level of sharing in mice were found to have an increased probability of being found in human repertoires; similarly, sequences more shared in humans were found more frequently in mice (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Sequences more shared in humans were found more frequently in mice.
source: In general, CDR3 sequences with a higher level of sharing in mice were found to have an increased probability of being found in human repertoires; similarly, sequences more shared in humans were found more frequently in mice (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: More than 25% of the public CDR3 sequences (found in all 11 young human subjects, or found in all 28 mice) were found also in at least one individual of the other species.
source: Of note, more than 25% of the public CDR3 sequences (found in all 11 young human subjects, or found in all 28 mice) were found also in at least one individual of the other species (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript reports this percentage and references Figure 2A.

claim: 86 cross-species (CS) public CDR3 sequences were public or relatively public in both mice (found in at least 25 of the 28 mice) and humans (found in all 11 young individuals).
source: We defined a set of cross-species (CS) public CDR3 sequences that were public or relatively public in both mice (found in at least 25 of the 28 mice) and humans (found in all 11 young individuals). All these 86 CS-public sequences contained the human Jβ2.7 or Jβ2.3 segments, and the mouse Jβ2.5 or Jβ2.7 segments.
evidence: The manuscript defines and counts CS-public sequences.

claim: All 86 CS-public sequences contained the human Jβ2.7 or Jβ2.3 segments, and the mouse Jβ2.5 or Jβ2.7 segments.
source: We defined a set of cross-species (CS) public CDR3 sequences that were public or relatively public in both mice (found in at least 25 of the 28 mice) and humans (found in all 11 young individuals). All these 86 CS-public sequences contained the human Jβ2.7 or Jβ2.3 segments, and the mouse Jβ2.5 or Jβ2.7 segments.
evidence: The manuscript reports the J segment usage of CS-public sequences.

claim: V usage in CS-public sequences was dominated by Vβ20.1 in humans, but a more diverse V usage was observed in mice.
source: V usage was dominated by Vβ20.1 in humans, but a more diverse V usage was observed in mice.
evidence: The manuscript reports the V segment usage patterns in CS-public sequences.

claim: CS-public CDR3 sequences manifested a significantly higher degree of connectivity in human and mouse networks than did CDR3 sequences that were public only in humans, only in mice or not public in either.
source: The CS-public CDR3 sequences manifested a significantly higher degree of connectivity in human and mouse networks than did CDR3 sequences that were public only in humans, only in mice or not public in either (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references supporting figures.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the mean degrees of CS-public sequences in mouse and human networks.
source: Moreover, we found a significant correlation between the mean degrees of CS-public sequences in mouse and human networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 3); CS-public sequences that have more neighbors in mouse networks also tended to have more neighbors in human networks, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved network structure.
evidence: The manuscript reports this correlation and references Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: CS-public sequences that have more neighbors in mouse networks also tended to have more neighbors in human networks, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved network structure.
source: Moreover, we found a significant correlation between the mean degrees of CS-public sequences in mouse and human networks (Figure 2—figure supplement 3); CS-public sequences that have more neighbors in mouse networks also tended to have more neighbors in human networks, suggesting an evolutionarily conserved network structure.
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from the correlation data.

claim: The frequency of CS-public sequences is not higher than that of other public sequences that are found only in humans or in mice.
source: We note that while CS-public sequences are central in network clusters, their frequency is not higher than that of other public sequences that are found only in humans or in mice.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about CS-public sequence frequencies.

claim: Simulated TCR repertoires contained a somewhat larger number of CS-public CDR3 sequences than observed in the experimental data (average of 221 ± 9 in the simulations, vs. 86 in the data).
source: The simulated repertoires contained a somewhat larger number of CS-public CDR3 sequences than observed in the experimental data (average of 221 ± 9 in the simulations, vs. 86 in the data).
evidence: The manuscript compares simulation results to experimental data.

claim: The simulated CS-public sequences contained the same restricted set of mouse and human J segments, which are highly similar between the two species (J2.7 mouse and human; J2.5 mouse/J2.3 human).
source: The simulated CS-public sequences contained the same restricted set of mouse and human J segments, which are highly similar between the two species (J2.7 mouse and human; J2.5 mouse/J2.3 human).
evidence: The manuscript reports the J segment usage in simulated CS-public sequences.

claim: Sequence homology of J segments contributes to the formation of CS-public TCRs, but is not sufficient by itself.
source: Thus, sequence homology of J segments contributes to the formation of CS-public TCRs, but is not sufficient by itself, and is accompanied by other mechanisms that induce bias in the recombination process (e.g. biased V segment usage, statistics of nucleotide deletions and insertions at V-D and D-J junctions).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from comparison of simulation and experimental data.

claim: 54 out of the 86 experimentally observed CS-public sequences were identical to simulated CS-public sequences, while 32 were not CS-public in the simulations.
source: We found that 54 out of the 86 experimentally observed CS-public sequences were identical to simulated CS-public sequences, while 32 were not CS-public in the simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports these counts from comparison of experimental and simulated data and references Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The partial overlap between simulations and data may result from inaccuracies in the assumptions of the simulations regarding the random TCR generation process, or indicate that selection mechanisms in the thymus and in the periphery further influence the existence of specific CS-public sequences.
source: The partial overlap between simulations and data may result from inaccuracies in the assumptions of the simulations regarding the random TCR generation process, or indicate that selection mechanisms in the thymus and in the periphery further influence the existence of specific CS-public sequences.
evidence: The manuscript proposes these explanations for the discrepancy between simulations and data.

claim: A network formed by the 1000 most public mouse sequences (found in >25 of the 28 mice) was highly connected, with 965 clustered nodes and 3387 edges.
source: A network formed by the 1000 most public mouse sequences (found in >25 of the 28 mice) was highly connected, with 965 clustered nodes and 3387 edges (Figure 3A).
evidence: The manuscript reports these network statistics and references Figure 3A.

claim: Networks formed by the 1000 most abundant private sequences (found in only one of the 28 mice) were very sparse, manifesting only 38 ± 15 clustered nodes and 20 ± 7 edges.
source: In contrast, networks formed by the 1000 most abundant private sequences (found in only one of the 28 mice) were very sparse, manifesting only 38 ± 15 clustered nodes and 20 ± 7 edges (mean ± SD, averaged over 28 mice).
evidence: The manuscript reports these network statistics for private sequences.

claim: A network formed by the 1000 most public human CDR3 sequences was highly connected (with 969 clustered nodes and 4398 edges).
source: Similarly, a network formed by the 1000 most public human CDR3 sequences was also highly connected (with 969 clustered nodes and 4398 edges, Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports these network statistics for human public sequences and references Figure 3B.

claim: The functional TCR is formed by a complex of TCR alpha and beta chains.
source: The functional TCR is formed by a complex of TCR alpha and beta chains (Davis and Bjorkman, 1988), hence one cannot attribute specific antigen recognition to CDR3β segments alone.
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about TCR structure.

claim: One cannot attribute specific antigen recognition to CDR3β segments alone.
source: The functional TCR is formed by a complex of TCR alpha and beta chains (Davis and Bjorkman, 1988), hence one cannot attribute specific antigen recognition to CDR3β segments alone.
evidence: The manuscript states this limitation based on TCR biology.

claim: TCRβ sequences that bind the same pMHC antigen do contain shared CDR3β sequence motifs.
source: Yet, TCRβ sequences that bind the same pMHC antigen do contain shared CDR3β sequence motifs (Klinger et al., 2015; Chen et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2017; Tickotsky et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: Out of 124 annotated sequences, 63 were either identical to one of the existing nodes (n = 11), or linked to an existing node by a Levenshtein distance of 1 (n = 52).
source: Out of the 124 annotated sequences, 63 were either identical to one of the existing nodes (n = 11), or linked to an existing node by a Levenshtein distance of 1 (n = 52).
evidence: The manuscript reports these counts from analysis of annotated sequences in networks.

claim: The clustered annotated nodes were found to be enriched with annotations related to self or self-like autoimmune, cancer or allograft reactions (self-related: 51/63 = 81% of network-clustered sequences vs. 85/124 = 69% in all 124 annotated sequences, compared to non-self: 12/63 = 19% in clusters vs. 39/124 = 31%; Fisher exact test p=0.0035).
source: The clustered annotated nodes were found to be enriched with annotations related to self or self-like autoimmune, cancer or allograft reactions (self-related: 51/63 = 81% of network-clustered sequences vs. 85/124 = 69% in all 124 annotated sequences, compared to non-self: 12/63 = 19% in clusters vs. 39/124 = 31%; Fisher exact test p=0.0035).
evidence: The manuscript reports this enrichment analysis with statistical test results.

claim: Sequences with a similar annotation tended to be linked in the same cluster.
source: We find that sequences with a similar annotation tended to be linked in the same cluster.
evidence: The manuscript states this observation about annotation clustering.

claim: Twelve sequences of tumor infiltrating regulatory T cells were found in cluster #2.
source: Examples include twelve sequences of tumor infiltrating regulatory T cells (Sainz-Perez et al., 2012) which were found in cluster #2; six COPD related CDR3 sequences (Motz et al., 2008) in cluster #6; and four CDR3 sequences connected with cluster #2 that were associated with type 1 diabetes in NOD mice in two different studies (Nakano et al., 1991; Tikochinski et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript provides this example with citations.

claim: Six COPD related CDR3 sequences were found in cluster #6.
source: Examples include twelve sequences of tumor infiltrating regulatory T cells (Sainz-Perez et al., 2012) which were found in cluster #2; six COPD related CDR3 sequences (Motz et al., 2008) in cluster #6; and four CDR3 sequences connected with cluster #2 that were associated with type 1 diabetes in NOD mice in two different studies (Nakano et al., 1991; Tikochinski et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript provides this example with citations.

claim: Four CDR3 sequences connected with cluster #2 were associated with type 1 diabetes in NOD mice in two different studies.
source: Examples include twelve sequences of tumor infiltrating regulatory T cells (Sainz-Perez et al., 2012) which were found in cluster #2; six COPD related CDR3 sequences (Motz et al., 2008) in cluster #6; and four CDR3 sequences connected with cluster #2 that were associated with type 1 diabetes in NOD mice in two different studies (Nakano et al., 1991; Tikochinski et al., 1999).
evidence: The manuscript provides this example with citations.

claim: Mouse CDR3 sequences associated with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) and collagen-induced arthritis (CIA) were connected to cluster #2.
source: However, different annotations can also be found in the same cluster (Figure 3A); for example, mouse CDR3 sequences associated with experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE; [Menezes et al., 2007]) and collagen-induced arthritis (CIA; [Osman et al., 1993]) were also connected to cluster #2.
evidence: The manuscript provides this example with citations and references Figure 3A.

claim: Many previously annotated self/self-like sequences of humans and mice were linked to clusters in the network of public human sequences.
source: Figure 3B shows that many previously annotated self/self-like sequences of humans and mice were also linked to clusters in the network of public human sequences.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and references Figure 3B.

claim: CDR3 clusters, which serve as repertoire foci, seem to be enriched with TCR sequences that are associated with self (or self-like) reactivities, whereas pathogen-associated TCR sequences are less clustered and so tend to be more evenly spread throughout sequence space.
source: Thus, the CDR3 clusters, which serve as repertoire foci, seem to be enriched with TCR sequences that are associated with self (or self-like) reactivities, whereas pathogen-associated TCR sequences are less clustered and so tend to be more evenly spread throughout sequence space.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the annotation analysis.

claim: Networks formed by DN CDR3 sequences were significantly less connected compared to splenic CD4+ T cells, which have undergone antigen selection.
source: We found that networks formed by DN CDR3 sequences were significantly less connected compared to splenic CD4+ T cells, which have undergone antigen selection (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this comparison and references Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: DN thymocytes and CD4+ spleen T cells manifested different levels of convergent recombination.
source: In addition, DN thymocytes and CD4+ spleen T cells manifested different levels of convergent recombination (Venturi et al., 2006, 2008).
evidence: The manuscript states this finding and cites relevant studies.

claim: Public CDR3 AA sequences in DN thymocytes were encoded on average by a low number of nucleotide (nt) sequences, whereas the same AA sequences were encoded by a much larger number of nt sequences in CD4+ splenic T cells.
source: Public CDR3 AA sequences in DN thymocytes were encoded on average by a low number of nucleotide (nt) sequences, whereas the same AA sequences were encoded by a much larger number of nt sequences in CD4+ splenic T cells (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The finding of relatively increased network clusters in T cells that have undergone antigen selection suggests that the CDR3 AA sequences that are found within clusters are positively selected.
source: The finding of relatively increased network clusters in T cells that have undergone antigen selection suggests that the CDR3 AA sequences that are found within clusters are positively selected; this antigen selection would extend any underlying physical bias generated during TCR DNA recombination in the thymus (Murugan et al., 2012; Ndifon et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from the comparison of DN and CD4+ T cells and cites relevant studies.

claim: Similarity networks formed by the top 1000 CDR3 sequences from Quad-KO mice were significantly less connected than those of the WT strain (C57BL/6) measured in the same set of experiments.
source: We found that similarity networks formed by the top 1000 CDR3 sequences from Quad-KO mice were significantly less connected than those of the WT strain (C57BL/6) measured in the same set of experiments (Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports this comparison and references Figure 4A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: MHC-dependent thymic selection plays a significant role in promoting the formation of dense clusters of TCR-similarity networks.
source: Together, these findings indicate that MHC-dependent thymic selection plays a significant role in promoting the formation of dense clusters of TCR-similarity networks.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the DN and Quad-KO experiments.

claim: Lack of MHC-dependent selection in DN thymocytes and in Quad-KO mice is associated with TCR networks of reduced connectivity.
source: Lack of MHC-dependent selection in DN thymocytes and in Quad-KO mice is associated with TCR networks of reduced connectivity; in contrast, TCRs that are subject to MHC selection form dense networks with a higher level of convergent recombination.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings from DN and Quad-KO experiments.

claim: TCRs that are subject to MHC selection form dense networks with a higher level of convergent recombination.
source: Lack of MHC-dependent selection in DN thymocytes and in Quad-KO mice is associated with TCR networks of reduced connectivity; in contrast, TCRs that are subject to MHC selection form dense networks with a higher level of convergent recombination.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the findings from DN and Quad-KO experiments.

claim: Recombination biases combined with clonal selection generate a TCR repertoire that is not uniform, but rather focused in specific regions of sequence space that are preferentially associated with self-related antigen-reactivities.
source: Thus, recombination biases combined with clonal selection generate a TCR repertoire that is not uniform, but rather focused in specific regions of sequence space that are preferentially associated with self-related antigen-reactivities.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the combined findings.

claim: The Quad-KO repertoires exhibited lower total frequency of the CS-public CDR3s compared with 28 WT mice (P value = 4.318e-09).
source: On the other hand, the Quad-KO repertoires exhibited lower total frequency of the CS-public CDR3s compared with both 28 WT mice (P value = 4.318e-09) and the Quad-WT mice (P value = 0.01781).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical comparison.

claim: The Quad-KO repertoires exhibited lower total frequency of the CS-public CDR3s compared with the Quad-WT mice (P value = 0.01781).
source: On the other hand, the Quad-KO repertoires exhibited lower total frequency of the CS-public CDR3s compared with both 28 WT mice (P value = 4.318e-09) and the Quad-WT mice (P value = 0.01781).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical comparison.

claim: Sequence homology of V and J germline segments between mice and humans and bias in the recombination process influence the probability for a sequence to be shared between the two species.
source: Together, these results indicate that, although sequence homology of V and J germline segments between mice and humans and bias in the recombination process influence the probability for a sequence to be shared between the two species, additional selection forces are influencing its abundance.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the CS-public sequence analysis.

claim: Additional selection forces beyond recombination bias are influencing the abundance of CS-public sequences.
source: Together, these results indicate that, although sequence homology of V and J germline segments between mice and humans and bias in the recombination process influence the probability for a sequence to be shared between the two species, additional selection forces are influencing its abundance.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the CS-public sequence analysis.

claim: Immunization with either p277 or OVA peptide resulted in repertoires that contained a set of expanded CDR3 sequences and had an increased abundance inequality.
source: We found that immunization with either peptide resulted in repertoires that contained a set of expanded CDR3 sequences and had an increased abundance inequality.
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding from immunization experiments.

claim: In vitro re-stimulation further increased inequality in immunized mice.
source: In vitro re-stimulation further increased inequality (Figure 5A–C and Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 5A–C and Supplementary file 3.

claim: The increased inequality after immunization was associated with the emergence of private clones that dominated the post-immunization repertoire, such that the relative weight of public clones was reduced.
source: This inequality was associated with the emergence of private clones that dominated the post-immunization repertoire, such that the relative weight of public clones was reduced (Figure 5E).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 5E.

claim: Immunization was associated with network disruption; the number of clustered nodes and the number of edges both fell after immunization in vivo and fell further after in vitro re-stimulation.
source: Interestingly, immunization was also associated with network disruption; the number of clustered nodes and the number of edges both fell after immunization in vivo and fell further after in vitro re-stimulation (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the increased inequality and the decreased network connectivity reversed spontaneously in the OVA-immunized mice 2 months following immunization.
source: Both the increased inequality and the decreased network connectivity reversed spontaneously in the OVA-immunized mice 2 months following immunization (Figure 5D,E (right), Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Repertoires in aged mice were more unequal and less connected than those of young individuals.
source: Similar to immunization, repertoires in aged mice (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and in aged humans (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) were more unequal and less connected than those of young individuals, and private CDR3 sequences became relatively more abundant with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references supporting figures.

claim: Repertoires in aged humans were more unequal and less connected than those of young individuals.
source: Similar to immunization, repertoires in aged mice (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and in aged humans (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) were more unequal and less connected than those of young individuals, and private CDR3 sequences became relatively more abundant with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references supporting figures.

claim: Private CDR3 sequences became relatively more abundant with age.
source: Similar to immunization, repertoires in aged mice (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2) and in aged humans (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 3) were more unequal and less connected than those of young individuals, and private CDR3 sequences became relatively more abundant with age (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The manuscript reports this finding and references Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation between the Gini Coefficient of TCR inequality and the number of connected nodes in TCR networks in mice (Spearman correlation = −0.661).
source: Altogether, we found a strong anti-correlation between the Gini Coefficient of TCR inequality and the number of connected nodes in TCR networks in mice (Figure 5F, Spearman correlation = −0.661) and in humans (Figure 5G, Spearman correlation = −0.865).
evidence: The manuscript reports this correlation coefficient and references Figure 5F.

claim: There is a strong anti-correlation between the Gini Coefficient of TCR inequality and the number of connected nodes in TCR networks in humans (Spearman correlation = −0.865).
source: Altogether, we found a strong anti-correlation between the Gini Coefficient of TCR inequality and the number of connected nodes in TCR networks in mice (Figure 5F, Spearman correlation = −0.661) and in humans (Figure 5G, Spearman correlation = −0.865).
evidence: The manuscript reports this correlation coefficient and references Figure 5G.

claim: The 1000 most abundant CDR3 sequences after checkpoint blockade are less connected than pre-treatment (p value<0.05 ranked Wilcox paired test).
source: Applying TCR similarity network analysis, we now show that the 1000 most abundant CDR3 sequences after check-point blockade are less connected than pre-treatment (p value<0.05 ranked Wilcox paired test, Figure 5H left); moreover, this reduction in connectivity was detected concurrently with a decrease in the number of public CDR3 sequences and an increase in the frequency of private ones (p-value=0.01947, ranked Wilcox paired test, Figure 5H right, Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical finding and references Figure 5H.

claim: After checkpoint blockade, there was a decrease in the number of public CDR3 sequences and an increase in the frequency of private ones (p-value=0.01947, ranked Wilcox paired test).
source: Applying TCR similarity network analysis, we now show that the 1000 most abundant CDR3 sequences after check-point blockade are less connected than pre-treatment (p value<0.05 ranked Wilcox paired test, Figure 5H left); moreover, this reduction in connectivity was detected concurrently with a decrease in the number of public CDR3 sequences and an increase in the frequency of private ones (p-value=0.01947, ranked Wilcox paired test, Figure 5H right, Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical finding and references Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: There was a strong increase of public (network promoting) TCRs in the peripheral blood of JIA patients compared to healthy donors (P value = 0.0006).
source: Finally, we analyzed TCR repertoires of patients with the autoimmune disease Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA)(Henderson et al., 2016). We found that there was a strong increase of public (network promoting) TCRs in the peripheral blood of JIA patients compared to healthy donors (P value = 0.0006, Figure 5I).
evidence: The manuscript reports this statistical finding and references Figure 5I.

claim: While immune perturbations such as immunization and aging lead to reduced levels of public clonotypes and a reduction in network connectivity, the autoimmune condition JIA is associated with an increased level of public clones which are putatively associated with self-antigens.
source: Thus, while immune perturbations such as immunization and aging lead to reduced levels of public clonotypes and a reduction in network connectivity, this specific autoimmune condition is associated with an increased level of public clones which are putatively associated with self-antigens.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the JIA analysis.

claim: In young, healthy individuals, the most abundant TCRβ CDR3 sequences are distributed unevenly in sequence-space, with clusters centered around public CDR3s, and in particular around CS-public sequences.
source: Our application of network analysis to TCRβ CDR3 sequencing data reveals a hitherto unrecognized structure of the TCR repertoire in both mice and humans: In young, healthy individuals, the most abundant TCRβ CDR3 sequences are distributed unevenly in sequence-space, with clusters centered around public CDR3s, and in particular around CS-public sequences, which are public both in mice and humans (Figure 5J top-right, even and focused repertoire).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this key finding and references Figure 5J.

claim: The clustering of the most abundant CDR3 sequences in young and healthy individuals results in a repertoire that is much more restricted than would be expected from the random process of TCR somatic recombination.
source: The clustering of the most abundant CDR3 sequences in young and healthy individuals results in a repertoire that is much more restricted than would be expected from the random process of TCR somatic recombination.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the network analysis findings.

claim: This basic network architecture is modified by immunization and aging due to the dominant expansion of more private CDR3 clonotypes.
source: This basic network architecture is modified by immunization and aging due to the dominant expansion of more private CDR3 clonotypes.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this finding from immunization and aging experiments.

claim: Public CDR3s that serve as hubs of the TCR networks become less prominent following immunization and aging, leading to reduced connectivity of the TCR networks combined with a more skewed repertoire.
source: Thus, public CDR3s that serve as hubs of the TCR networks become less prominent, leading to reduced connectivity of the TCR networks combined with a more skewed repertoire (Figure 5J bottom-left, skewed and spread repertoire).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this finding and references Figure 5J.

claim: Network organization and repertoire evenness are restored with the resolution of immune responses.
source: We find that network organization and repertoire evenness are restored with the resolution of immune responses.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from the OVA immunization time course.

claim: Incomplete resolution of immune responses throughout life may lead to accumulation of changes in the TCR repertoire that eventually result in the skewed and spread (less clustered) repertoires observed in aged individuals.
source: It might be the case that incomplete resolution of immune responses throughout life lead to accumulation of changes in the TCR repertoire that eventually result in the skewed and spread (less clustered) repertoires that we observe in aged individuals.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: TCR repertoires from patients with the autoimmune condition JIA showed increased levels of public TCR sequences.
source: Interestingly, TCR repertoires from patients with the autoimmune condition JIA showed increased levels of public TCR sequences.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from JIA patient analysis.

claim: The level of network connectivity, frequency of public TCRs and repertoire evenness are linked to each other, and are concurrently modulated by the individual's immune state (disease/immunization/aging).
source: Taken together, our analysis supports the idea that the level of network connectivity, frequency of public TCRs and repertoire evenness are linked to each other, and are concurrently modulated by the individual's immune state (disease/immunization/ aging).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the combined findings.

claim: MHC-dependent antigen selection contributes to the formation of dense networks.
source: Mechanistically, we found that MHC-dependent antigen selection contributes to the formation of dense networks, since reduced network connectivity was observed in pre-selection DN thymocytes and also by inhibiting MHC-dependent selection, in the Quad-KO mice.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes this mechanistic finding.

claim: Preferential selection and increased survival of T cells that carry specific CDR3 sequences that recognize self-antigens presented by MHC molecules can explain the formation of dense networks.
source: These results can be explained by preferential selection and increased survival, in both the thymus and periphery, of T cells that carry specific CDR3 sequences that recognize self-antigens presented by MHC molecules.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this explanation for the network formation mechanism.

claim: Different T cell clones, which carry different CDR3 nt sequences but encode the same AA sequence, would appear to enjoy a common selective advantage and accumulate in the peripheral repertoire.
source: Different T cell clones, which carry different CDR3 nt sequences but encode the same AA sequence, would appear to enjoy a common selective advantage and accumulate in the peripheral repertoire.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism to explain convergent recombination.

claim: This mechanism can explain the observations of increased convergent recombination in splenic CD4+ T cells compared to DN thymocytes.
source: This mechanism can explain our observations of increased convergent recombination in splenic CD4+ T cells compared to DN thymocytes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript links the proposed mechanism to the observed data and references Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Antigen selection can account for the enhanced network connectivity of TCRs that differ by one AA in their CDR3 sequences; such related CDR3 sequences may be selected by the same peptide-MHC complex, albeit with different affinities.
source: Antigen selection can also account for the enhanced network connectivity of TCRs that differ by one AA in their CDR3 sequences; such related CDR3 sequences may be selected by the same peptide-MHC complex, albeit with different affinities (Moss et al., 1991; Serana et al., 2009; Zoete et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this explanation and cites supporting studies.

claim: MHC-antigen selection of public CDR3 sequences takes place on a background of biases in the biophysical process of DNA recombination.
source: MHC-antigen selection of public CDR3 sequences takes place on a background of biases in the biophysical process of DNA recombination (Elhanati et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript states this and cites a relevant study.

claim: Combined, recombination biases and MHC-antigen selection lead to the formation of dense network clusters of the most abundant public TCR sequences.
source: Combined, these processes lead to the formation of dense network clusters of the most abundant public TCR sequences, as we report here.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the combined mechanisms.

claim: The most abundant private TCR sequences generate poorly connected networks.
source: In contrast, the most abundant private TCR sequences generate poorly connected networks.
evidence: The manuscript states this finding from the network analysis.

claim: BCR networks have a distinct structure resulting from the SHM process, in which abundance and degree are correlated, which is not the case in TCR networks.
source: Thus, dominant and public T cell clonotypes have a higher sequence similarity than non-dominant and private ones. In contrast, BCR networks have a distinct structure resulting from the SHM process, in which abundance and degree are correlated, which is not the case in TCR networks.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts TCR and BCR network structures.

claim: The finding that TCR CDR3 networks include identical and related sequences that are shared by most individuals of the same species and even cross the species divide between mice and humans suggests the likelihood of some fundamental evolutionary advantage in such sequences.
source: Our finding that TCR CDR3 networks include identical and related sequences that are not confined to individuals but are shared by most individuals of the same species and even cross the species divide between mice and humans, suggests the likelihood of some fundamental evolutionary advantage in such sequences.
evidence: The manuscript draws this inference from the cross-species conservation findings.

claim: The same or very similar CDR3β sequences are frequently observed within repertoires of T cells specific for a given antigen, in combination with flexible or preferential pairing with TCRα.

evidence: The manuscript cites studies supporting this claim.

claim: T cell clones bearing the conserved, CS-public, CDR3 sequences may recognize similar antigenic epitopes that are conserved across species.
source: Hence, we hypothesize that T cell clones bearing the conserved, CS-public, CDR3 sequences recognize similar antigenic epitopes that are conserved across species.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on the CS-public sequence findings.

claim: CS-public antigens may be derived from evolutionarily conserved regions of self proteins, forming a core of T cell reactivities to specific self epitopes, with potential implications for self-maintenance, autoimmunity and cancer.
source: These antigens may be derived from evolutionarily conserved regions of self proteins, forming a core of T cell reactivities to specific self epitopes, with potential implications for self-maintenance, autoimmunity and cancer.

claim: T lymphocytes 'focus their attention' to specific regions in sequence space.
source: Our results indicate that T lymphocytes 'focus their attention' to specific regions in sequence space.

claim: The CDR3 is the most diverse segment of the TCR and is positioned to interact with the antigenic peptide epitope presented by an MHC molecule.
source: We focused on the CDR3 (complementary determining region 3) amino acid (AA) sequence of the TCRβ chain, which is the most diverse segment of the TCR and is positioned to interact with the antigenic peptide epitope presented by an MHC molecule (Davis and Bjorkman, 1988).
evidence: The manuscript cites established knowledge about CDR3 function.
